# Project: A Software-Defined Radio Receiver {#sec-sdr}

This is the last project of the book and the largest. After the modem
(@sec-modem) and the pedalboard (@sec-pedalboard), it tells the story of a whole radio
receiver, from the antenna to the loudspeaker, and builds everything that *can* be built
in software. It uses the whole book, and it explains from the beginning the things
that the other chapters did not need: why a signal is sent on a carrier, how
information is written on it, and what a broadcast station actually transmits.
Like the rest of the book it is executable: the "radio signal" that we receive is
created by the code of the chapter, and every claim is checked on it.

By the end you should be able to:

- say what a software-defined radio is, what it gains over a traditional receiver,
  and which parts of a radio are still analog;
- explain why information travels on a carrier, and how amplitude and frequency
  modulation write a message on it;
- describe the signal of a stereo FM broadcast station, from the audio to the
  composite signal that modulates the carrier;
- represent a radio signal by its complex envelope, the in-phase and quadrature
  samples that an SDR delivers, and explain why this needs about a hundred times
  fewer samples than sampling the radio-frequency signal itself;
- generate a synthetic "capture" of the FM band, as a software-defined radio would
  record it.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Setup: imports, constants and the audio players of the HTML edition"
import io, base64, wave
from fractions import Fraction
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import FancyBboxPatch, FancyArrowPatch
from scipy import signal, special

rng = np.random.default_rng(88)
plt.rcParams["figure.figsize"] = (7, 3)
plt.rcParams["axes.grid"] = True
plt.rcParams["grid.alpha"] = 0.3

def wav_base64(x, rate):
    """16-bit WAV file (mono, or stereo if x has two columns) as a base64 string."""
    x = np.asarray(x)
    pcm = np.round(np.clip(x, -1, 1) * 32767).astype("<i2")
    buf = io.BytesIO()
    with wave.open(buf, "wb") as w:
        w.setnchannels(1 if x.ndim == 1 else x.shape[1]); w.setsampwidth(2); w.setframerate(rate)
        w.writeframes(pcm.tobytes())
    return base64.b64encode(buf.getvalue()).decode()

class Clips:
    """Labelled audio players, shown in the HTML edition (the same trick as the GIF animations)."""
    def __init__(self, clips, rate):
        self.html = "".join(
            f'<div style="margin:0.4em 0"><div style="font-size:0.9em">{label}</div>'
            f'<audio controls preload="none" src="data:audio/wav;base64,{wav_base64(x, rate)}"></audio></div>'
            for label, x in clips.items())

    def _repr_html_(self):
        return self.html

def welch_psd(x, rate, nperseg=4096):
    """Welch estimate of the power spectral density (Hann window, 50 % overlap), in units^2 per Hz.

    A complex signal gives a two-sided result with the frequencies centred on zero; a real one, a
    one-sided result. (scipy.signal.welch fails on signals of more than about 10^5 samples in the
    browser, where array sizes are 32-bit, so we write it: it is a loop over the segments.)"""
    w = np.hanning(nperseg)
    hop = nperseg // 2
    n_seg = (len(x) - nperseg) // hop + 1
    if np.iscomplexobj(x):
        acc = sum(np.abs(np.fft.fft(x[k * hop:k * hop + nperseg] * w)) ** 2 for k in range(n_seg))
        f, P = np.fft.fftfreq(nperseg, 1 / rate), acc / (n_seg * rate * np.sum(w ** 2))
        order = np.argsort(f)
        return f[order], P[order]
    acc = sum(np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x[k * hop:k * hop + nperseg] * w)) ** 2 for k in range(n_seg))
    P = acc / (n_seg * rate * np.sum(w ** 2))
    P[1:-1] *= 2                                               # one-sided: fold the negative frequencies in
    return np.fft.rfftfreq(nperseg, 1 / rate), P

def psd_db(x, rate, nperseg=4096):
    """Power spectral density of a (complex) signal in dB, with the frequencies centred on zero."""
    f, P = welch_psd(x, rate, nperseg)
    return f, 10 * np.log10(P + 1e-30)

# Our estimator agrees with SciPy's on a signal that SciPy can handle.
x_chk = rng.normal(size=20_000) + 1j * rng.normal(size=20_000)
f_ours, P_ours = welch_psd(x_chk, 1000.0, 512)
f_sp, P_sp = signal.welch(x_chk, 1000.0, window=np.hanning(512), nperseg=512, detrend=False, return_onesided=False)
assert np.allclose(P_ours, P_sp[np.argsort(f_sp)], rtol=1e-6)
```

## Why a radio is moving into the computer {#sec-sdr-trend}

Almost everything that processes signals has been moving from analog to digital
for sixty years. Telephone exchanges stopped switching voltages and began
switching numbers; the long-playing record gave way to the compact disc; film
cameras to sensors with converters; analog television to digital broadcasting;
the telephone in the pocket is, for the most part, a signal processor that also
has a radio attached to it. The reason is always the same, and it is the reason
why the first thirteen chapters of this book exist. Once a signal is a sequence
of numbers, processing it is a program, and a program has properties that a
circuit does not:

- **Repeatability.** Two analog filters built with the same design differ,
  because resistors and capacitors have tolerances, and each one drifts with
  temperature and age. A digital filter is a list of coefficients, and every copy
  is the same, today and in ten years.
- **Flexibility.** Changing the behaviour of a circuit means soldering. Changing
  a program means editing it, even after the product has been sold.
- **Functions that circuits cannot give.** Exactly linear-phase filters
  (@sec-filter-design), delays of fractions of a sample (@sec-sampling), adaptive
  filters that learn their coefficients, the FFT of the last second, an
  automatic gain that looks into the future: all are natural in a program and
  impossible or very costly in analog hardware.
- **No accumulation of noise.** An analog signal that is amplified, filtered,
  recorded and copied picks up noise at every step. A digital signal is copied
  without losing a bit, and noise enters only where the world is converted into
  numbers.
- **Cost that follows the chips.** Processors and converters become cheaper and
  faster every year; capacitors and coils do not become smaller.
- **Testing and simulation.** A system that is software can be simulated, tested
  with a million cases, versioned and shared. This chapter is an example: it
  contains a complete radio that nobody has to build.

Two of these claims can be shown in a few lines.

```{python}
# (1) Repeatability: the cut-off of an RC low-pass is 1/(2 pi R C); with parts of 5 % tolerance
#     every copy of the "same" filter is different. A digital filter has no tolerance.
n_copies = 10_000
R = 10e3 * rng.uniform(0.95, 1.05, n_copies)               # 10 kOhm, +-5 %
C = 1e-9 * rng.uniform(0.95, 1.05, n_copies)               # 1 nF, +-5 %
fc = 1 / (2 * np.pi * R * C)
nominal = 1 / (2 * np.pi * 10e3 * 1e-9)
spread = (fc.max() - fc.min()) / nominal
print(f"analog RC filter, nominal cut-off {nominal / 1e3:.2f} kHz: copies range over {100 * spread:.1f} % of it")
assert spread > 0.15                                        # parts of 5 % give copies that differ by 15 % or more

# (2) Noise accumulation: copy a signal through N analog stages, each adding noise 60 dB below it.
x = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 440 * np.arange(48_000) / 48_000)
analog = x.copy()
for stage in range(1, 11):
    analog = analog + rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(np.mean(x ** 2)) * 10 ** (-60 / 20), len(x))
    if stage in (1, 10):
        snr = 10 * np.log10(np.sum(x ** 2) / np.sum((analog - x) ** 2))
        print(f"after {stage:2d} analog copies: SNR {snr:.1f} dB")
digital = x.astype(np.float32).copy()
for stage in range(10):
    digital = digital.copy()                                # a bit-exact copy, ten times
print(f"after 10 digital copies: identical = {np.array_equal(digital, x.astype(np.float32))}")
assert np.array_equal(digital, x.astype(np.float32))
assert 49 < snr < 51                                        # 60 dB - 10 log10(10) = 50 dB
```

The costs are the converters and the power they need: a converter has a limited
number of bits (@sec-quantization) and a limited rate, and the faster and
more precise it is, the more energy it uses. The history of radio receivers is
the story of the converter moving *towards the antenna*, as far as these limits
allow:

| Era | What is digital | What is still analog |
|---|---|---|
| Valve and transistor radios | nothing | everything |
| Radios with digital tuning | the display and the tuning logic | the signal path |
| Digital audio processing in the receiver | tone control, equalisation, decoding of the stereo signal | the radio-frequency part and the demodulation |
| Mobile phones | everything after the first conversion to a low frequency (the *baseband*) | the antenna, amplifier and first mixer |
| Software-defined radio | everything after a converter that samples a band of the spectrum | the antenna, the amplifier, the tuner and the converter |

This chapter lives in the last row.

## What is a software-defined radio {#sec-sdr-what}

A **software-defined radio** (SDR) is a radio in which the functions that decide
what the radio *is*, such as selecting a channel, demodulating, decoding, are
carried out by a programmable processor and not by fixed hardware
[@mitola1995; @reed2002; @collins2018]. The same device can then be a broadcast
receiver, an aircraft tracker or the radio of a weather satellite, changing only
the program. @fig-sdr-chains compares a traditional receiver with an SDR.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sdr-chains
#| fig-cap: "A traditional superheterodyne receiver (top) and a software-defined radio (bottom). Orange blocks are analog hardware, blue blocks are computation. In the SDR the analog part ends in the converter, and everything the radio does (choosing the channel, demodulating, processing the audio) is a program."
def draw_chain(ax, blocks, y):
    """Draw a row of boxes joined by arrows; each block is (label, 'analog' or 'digital')."""
    x, w, gap = 0.0, 1.0, 0.32
    colours = {"analog": "#f4c27a", "digital": "#9ec5e8"}
    for i, (label, kind) in enumerate(blocks):
        ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x, y - 0.32), w, 0.64, boxstyle="round,pad=0.02,rounding_size=0.08",
                                    fc=colours[kind], ec="0.25", lw=0.8))
        ax.text(x + w / 2, y, label, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.4)
        if i:
            ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x - gap, y), (x, y), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=7, lw=0.8, color="0.25"))
        x += w + gap
    return x - gap

traditional = [("antenna", "analog"), ("RF filter\n+ amplifier", "analog"), ("mixer\n(oscillator)", "analog"),
               ("IF filter", "analog"), ("analog\ndemodulator", "analog"), ("audio\namplifier", "analog"),
               ("loud-\nspeaker", "analog")]
software = [("antenna", "analog"), ("RF filter\n+ amplifier", "analog"), ("mixer\n(oscillator)", "analog"),
            ("anti-alias\nfilter", "analog"), ("ADC", "analog"), ("channel filter\n+ decimation", "digital"),
            ("demodulation\n+ stereo", "digital"), ("audio\nprocessing", "digital"), ("DAC +\nspeaker", "analog")]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.4, 2.5))
width = max(draw_chain(ax, traditional, 1.5), draw_chain(ax, software, 0.35))
ax.set(xlim=(-0.1, width + 0.1), ylim=(-0.1, 2.0))
ax.axis("off")
ax.text(-0.05, 1.95, "traditional receiver", fontsize=8, weight="bold", va="top")
ax.text(-0.05, 0.8, "software-defined radio", fontsize=8, weight="bold", va="top")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The figure shows what is left of the analog world. Five things cannot be
replaced by a program, at least not yet:

| Block | What it does | Why it is still analog |
|---|---|---|
| Antenna | converts the electromagnetic wave into a voltage | it is a piece of metal whose size is tied to the wavelength |
| RF filter | removes strong signals far from the band of interest | a strong station nearby would saturate the converter |
| Low-noise amplifier | makes the antenna signal larger than the noise of what follows | the receiver's noise is fixed by its first stage |
| Mixer and oscillator | move the band of interest to a low frequency | no converter is fast enough to sample 100 MHz carriers *and* precise enough |
| Converter (ADC) | turns the voltage into numbers | it is the border, the place where the analog world ends |

Why the mixer? A radio signal is a narrow band of frequencies around a high
carrier. FM broadcasting uses carriers between 88 and 108 MHz. We could try to
sample the antenna voltage directly, but the sampling theorem (@sec-sampling) asks
for more than twice the highest frequency, so more than 216 million samples per
second, with a converter whose analog input must also be precise at 108 MHz. It is
possible, with expensive converters and a lot of power. The usual solution is
cheaper: the mixer moves the band that interests us to be centred on zero
frequency, and then the converter needs to cover only the *width* of the band.
We make the comparison for a typical USB receiver, which samples 0.96 million
complex samples per second (we use this number for the whole chapter):

```{python}
f_max = 108e6                                              # top of the FM band, Hz
direct_rate = 2 * f_max                                    # real samples per second to sample the RF itself
iq_rate = 0.96e6                                           # complex samples per second after the mixer
print(f"sampling the radio frequency: {direct_rate / 1e6:.0f} million real samples per second")
print(f"I/Q after the mixer: {iq_rate / 1e6:.2f} million complex = {2 * iq_rate / 1e6:.2f} million real samples per second")
print(f"ratio: {direct_rate / (2 * iq_rate):.0f} times fewer")
assert direct_rate / (2 * iq_rate) > 100
```

It is a hundred times fewer samples. The price is that what the converter
delivers is not an ordinary signal but a *pair* of signals, called I and Q, which
we define in @sec-sdr-iq. This was the trick that made SDRs cheap: in the early
2010s it was discovered that some inexpensive USB receivers for digital
television could deliver these raw samples to a computer, and with them a
generation of students and amateurs began to receive aircraft, satellites and
radio stations with a program.

## The project {#sec-sdr-project}

We build a **receiver for FM stereo broadcasting**, the music and talk stations
of 88–108 MHz. It is a good project for three reasons: everybody knows what the
result must sound like; the signal is rich, with a carrier, a modulation,
a stereo multiplex and an emphasis curve, so that nearly all of the book is used;
and the whole receiver is within the reach of a program.

There is no antenna in a book. What we do instead is to *build the signal that
a software-defined radio delivers*: an array of complex numbers, sampled at
0.96 MHz, that contains four stations, noise, a small frequency error of the tuner
and the roughness of an 8-bit converter. We build it with the same kind of
formulas that a real station uses, so that the receiver cannot tell the difference.
In fact the capture is stored in the *format* of a real dongle (interleaved
unsigned bytes), and the receiver reads it as it would read a file recorded
from an antenna: replacing one by the other is Exercise 8.

The plan of the project is the following.

| Stage | What we do | Tools of the book |
|---|---|---|
| **1. The antenna** | Synthesise the capture: four stations, noise, tuner error, 8-bit converter | modulation, noise, quantisation |
| 2. Spectrum | Look at the band, find the stations, measure the tuner error | DFT, windows, PSD |
| 3. Tuning | Move the chosen station to zero frequency | complex exponentials |
| 4. Channel selection | Filter out the neighbours and reduce the rate | FIR design, multirate |
| 5. Demodulation | Recover the composite signal from the phase | instantaneous frequency |
| 6. Stereo decoding | Find the pilot, regenerate the subcarrier, separate L and R | filters, phase-locked loop |
| 7. Audio | De-emphasis and resampling to 48 kHz | IIR filters, multirate |
| 8. Measurements | Selectivity, SNR against signal strength, the FM threshold | noise, estimation |
| 9. Real data | Run the receiver on a recording from a real dongle | everything |

Before building the antenna signal we need to understand what a station puts on
it. That is the subject of the next two sections.

## How information travels by radio {#sec-sdr-modulation}

### Why a carrier

A voice has frequencies between 100 Hz and a few kHz. We could think of sending
it directly, as a signal that varies at those frequencies. Two things prevent it.

The first is the **antenna**. An antenna radiates efficiently when its length is
a sizable fraction of the wavelength $\lambda = c/f$ (a quarter of it for a simple
whip), where $c \approx 3\times10^8$ m/s is the speed of light.

```{python}
c_light = 299_792_458.0
for name, f in (("a voice, 1 kHz", 1e3), ("AM broadcasting, 1 MHz", 1e6), ("FM broadcasting, 100 MHz", 100e6),
                ("a mobile phone, 2 GHz", 2e9)):
    lam = c_light / f
    print(f"{name:26s} wavelength {lam:12.2f} m, quarter-wave antenna {lam / 4:10.3f} m")
assert abs(c_light / 100e6 / 4 - 0.75) < 0.01               # a 75 cm whip for the FM band
```

An antenna for a 1 kHz signal would be 75 kilometres long. At 100 MHz it is a
whip of 75 cm. Raising the frequency of the signal solves the antenna.

The second is **sharing**. If every station radiated its voice directly, they
would all occupy the same frequencies and hear each other. By shifting each message
to a different place of the spectrum, a different **carrier frequency**, many
stations can transmit at once through the same air and a receiver can pick one by
tuning. This is **frequency-division multiplexing**, the same idea as the one of
the telephone line of @sec-modem, now with the sky as the channel.

A **carrier** is a sinusoid $A\cos(2\pi f_ct)$ with the frequency $f_c$ chosen for
the station, and **modulation** is the act of changing one of its three
parameters (amplitude, frequency or phase) according to the message $m(t)$, the
signal that we want to send. Only the changes carry information; an unmodulated
carrier says only that a station exists.

### Amplitude modulation and frequency modulation

The simplest way to write a message on a carrier is to vary its **amplitude**:
$$
s_{\mathrm{AM}}(t) = \big(1 + \mu\,m(t)\big)\cos(2\pi f_ct),
\qquad |m(t)| \le 1,\ 0 < \mu \le 1.
$$
This is **amplitude modulation** (AM), used in medium-wave broadcasting. The
envelope of the carrier is the message. The alternative is to vary the
**frequency**. In **frequency modulation** (FM) the amplitude is constant and the
*instantaneous frequency* follows the message:
$$
s_{\mathrm{FM}}(t) = A\cos\big(\varphi(t)\big),
\qquad
\varphi(t) = 2\pi f_ct + 2\pi k_f\int_{-\infty}^{t}m(\tau)\,d\tau .
$$
The instantaneous frequency is the derivative of the phase divided by $2\pi$,
$f_i(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\varphi'(t) = f_c + k_f\,m(t)$: it moves around $f_c$ by an
amount proportional to the message. The constant $k_f$ (in Hz per unit of $m$) is
the **sensitivity**, and the largest excursion $\Delta f = k_f\max|m|$ is the
**frequency deviation**. A broadcast station uses $\Delta f = 75$ kHz.

@fig-am-fm shows the same message, a 500 Hz tone, on both. We use a carrier of
8 kHz and a sampling rate of 64 kHz, a scaled-down version of the 100 MHz of the
real band so that we can see the details (the ideas do not depend on the scale).

```{python}
#| label: fig-am-fm
#| fig-cap: "A 500 Hz tone modulated on a carrier of 8 kHz, in amplitude (left) and in frequency with a deviation of 2 kHz (right). Top: waveforms; the AM envelope follows the message while the FM envelope is constant and the waves crowd and spread. Bottom: spectra in dB; AM has a carrier and two sidelines, FM has many lines around the carrier."
fs_demo, fc_demo, fm_demo = 64_000, 8_000, 500
t = np.arange(fs_demo) / fs_demo                             # one second
message = np.cos(2 * np.pi * fm_demo * t)
am = (1 + 0.8 * message) * np.cos(2 * np.pi * fc_demo * t)
kf_demo = 2_000                                              # deviation 2 kHz
phase = 2 * np.pi * fc_demo * t + 2 * np.pi * kf_demo * np.cumsum(message) / fs_demo
fm = np.cos(phase)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(7.4, 4.2))
for col, (x, name) in enumerate(((am, "AM"), (fm, "FM"))):
    axes[0, col].plot(t[:256] * 1e3, x[:256], lw=0.8)
    axes[0, col].plot(t[:256] * 1e3, 1 + 0.8 * message[:256] if name == "AM" else np.ones(256), "--", color="C3", lw=0.7)
    axes[0, col].set(title=name, xlabel="time [ms]")
    X = 20 * np.log10(np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x * np.hanning(len(x)))) / len(x) * 4 + 1e-6)
    axes[1, col].plot(np.fft.rfftfreq(len(x), 1 / fs_demo) / 1e3, X, lw=0.7)
    axes[1, col].set(xlim=(0, 16), ylim=(-100, 5), xlabel="frequency [kHz]", ylabel="dB")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# AM with a tone has exactly three lines: the carrier and two sidelines of relative amplitude mu/2.
X = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(am)) / (len(am) / 2)
k_c = fc_demo * len(am) // fs_demo
lines = X[[k_c - fm_demo, k_c, k_c + fm_demo]]
print("AM lines (carrier - fm, carrier, carrier + fm):", np.round(lines, 4))
assert np.allclose(lines, [0.4, 1.0, 0.4], atol=1e-6)         # mu = 0.8: sidelines of mu/2
assert np.max(X[(np.arange(len(X)) < k_c - fm_demo - 1) | (np.arange(len(X)) > k_c + fm_demo + 1)]) < 1e-9
```

The AM spectrum has three lines: the carrier, and two *sidelines* at
$f_c \pm f_m$ (the message shifted up and down), each of amplitude $\mu/2$ of the
carrier. It is simple and costs little, but noise from lightning, motors and
electronic equipment adds to the *amplitude* of the signal and is demodulated with
it. FM is much more robust, because the receiver can ignore the amplitude
completely and look only at the frequency: at the cost of using more spectrum,
as we are going to measure.

### The spectrum of FM

FM is not linear in the message: the spectrum of an FM signal is not the spectrum
of the message shifted. But for a pure tone it is a classic, and exact.

::: {#prp-fm-tone}
## FM with a tone

Let $A > 0$, $f_c > 0$, $f_m > 0$, $\beta \ge 0$ and
$s(t) = A\cos\big(2\pi f_ct + \beta\sin(2\pi f_mt)\big)$, the FM signal of the
message $m(t) = \cos(2\pi f_mt - \pi/2)$ with modulation index
$\beta = \Delta f/f_m$. Then
$$
\begin{aligned}
s(t) &= A\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}J_n(\beta)\cos\big(2\pi(f_c + nf_m)t\big),\\
J_n(\beta) &= \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos(n\theta - \beta\sin\theta)\,d\theta,
\end{aligned}
$$
where $J_n$ is the **Bessel function** of the first kind of order $n$. They
satisfy $J_{-n} = (-1)^nJ_n$ and $\sum_nJ_n(\beta)^2 = 1$.
:::

::: {.proof}
The function $\theta \mapsto e^{j\beta\sin\theta}$ is smooth and $2\pi$-periodic,
so it is the sum of its Fourier series (@sec-advanced-proofs),
$e^{j\beta\sin\theta} = \sum_nc_ne^{jn\theta}$ with
$c_n = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}e^{j(\beta\sin\theta - n\theta)}d\theta$. The
imaginary part of the integrand, $\sin(\beta\sin\theta - n\theta)$, is odd in
$\theta$, so $c_n$ is real and equal to $J_n(\beta)$. Put
$\theta = 2\pi f_mt$ and take the real part of $Ae^{j2\pi f_ct}e^{j\beta\sin\theta}$:
the formula follows, because the $J_n$ are real.

For the symmetry, replace $\theta$ by $\theta + \pi$ in the integral of $J_{-n}$:
$\sin(\theta + \pi) = -\sin\theta$ and the cosine acquires the factor $(-1)^n$.
Finally $|e^{j\beta\sin\theta}| = 1$, and Parseval's identity for the Fourier
series gives $\sum_nc_n^2 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int 1\,d\theta = 1$.
:::

So an FM tone has *infinitely many* lines, spaced by $f_m$ around the carrier,
with amplitudes $|J_n(\beta)|$; the power is shared among them, and, since
$\sum J_n^2 = 1$, it does not depend on $\beta$: *the modulation moves power from
the carrier to the sidelines, it does not create it*. How many lines matter? The
Bessel functions decay quickly for $|n|$ larger than $\beta$, and a classic rule of
thumb, **Carson's rule** [@carson1922], says that nearly all of the power is within
the band of width
$$
B_{\mathrm{Carson}} = 2(\Delta f + f_m) = 2f_m(\beta + 1),
$$
that is, in the lines with $|n| \le \beta + 1$. It is a rule, not a theorem, so we
test it: we check the proposition on the complex signal $e^{j\beta\sin\theta}$,
whose lines are exactly the $J_n$ (the real signal has half of each at $\pm f_c$),
and compute the power inside the Carson band.

```{python}
#| label: fig-fm-spectrum
#| fig-cap: "Lines of the spectrum of an FM tone for three modulation indices, as measured on the signal (dots) and given by the Bessel functions $J_n(\\beta)$ (crosses). The shaded band is Carson's: $|n| \\le \\beta + 1$. A larger index spreads the power over more lines."
fs_t, f_m_t, N_t = 48_000, 1_000, 48_000                       # one second: 1000 whole periods
tt = np.arange(N_t) / fs_t
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(7.4, 2.6), sharey=True)
for ax, beta in zip(axes, (0.5, 2.0, 5.0)):
    z = np.exp(1j * beta * np.sin(2 * np.pi * f_m_t * tt))      # complex envelope of the FM tone
    Z = np.fft.fft(z) / N_t
    n = np.arange(-12, 13)
    measured = np.abs(Z[(n * f_m_t * N_t // fs_t) % N_t])
    assert np.allclose(measured, np.abs(special.jv(n, beta)), atol=1e-12)          # @prp-fm-tone
    assert abs(np.sum(np.abs(Z) ** 2) - 1) < 1e-12                                 # sum of J_n^2 is 1
    inside = np.abs(n) <= beta + 1
    carson_power = np.sum(special.jv(n[inside], beta) ** 2)
    print(f"beta = {beta}: lines with |n| <= {int(beta + 1)} carry {100 * carson_power:.2f} % of the power")
    assert carson_power > 0.98
    ax.axvspan(-beta - 1.5, beta + 1.5, color="C1", alpha=0.15)
    ax.plot(n, measured, "o", ms=4)
    ax.plot(n, np.abs(special.jv(n, beta)), "x", ms=6, color="C3")
    ax.set(title=f"$\\beta$ = {beta}", xlabel="line number $n$")
axes[0].set_ylabel("amplitude relative to the carrier")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

In every case the Carson band contains more than 98 % of the power. For a music
station, the message is not a tone but a signal of up to $W = 15$ kHz; the same
rule, with the deviation of 75 kHz, gives
$B = 2(75 + 15) = 180$ kHz. This is why stations are spaced by 200 kHz in the
band: a channel is 200 kHz wide, about as much as the signal needs.

### The complex envelope: I and Q {#sec-sdr-iq}

A radio signal is real and has a high frequency, but its information is in a
narrow band around the carrier. The tool that separates the two is the **complex
envelope**. Any real signal of the form
$$
s(t) = I(t)\cos(2\pi f_ct) - Q(t)\sin(2\pi f_ct)
$$
with $I$ and $Q$ real signals of bandwidth $W < f_c$, can be written
$s(t) = \operatorname{Re}\{z(t)\,e^{j2\pi f_ct}\}$ with $z(t) = I(t) + jQ(t)$, the
complex envelope (@sec-complex-numbers). $I$ is called the **in-phase** and $Q$
the **quadrature** component. For FM, $z(t) = A\,e^{j2\pi k_f\int m}$: a
complex number of constant modulus whose angle carries the message. The receiver
recovers $z$ with the circuit of @fig-sdr-chains: the mixer.

::: {#prp-quadrature-mixer}
## The quadrature mixer

Let $s(t) = I(t)\cos(2\pi f_ct) - Q(t)\sin(2\pi f_ct)$ with $I$ and $Q$ real and
with spectra contained in $|f| < W$, $W < f_c$. Then
$$
\begin{aligned}
2s(t)\cos(2\pi f_ct) &= I(t) + I(t)\cos(4\pi f_ct) - Q(t)\sin(4\pi f_ct),\\
-2s(t)\sin(2\pi f_ct) &= Q(t) - I(t)\sin(4\pi f_ct) - Q(t)\cos(4\pi f_ct),
\end{aligned}
$$
and the terms at $2f_c$ have their spectra in $2f_c - W < |f| < 2f_c + W$. A
low-pass filter with cut-off between $W$ and $2f_c - W$ therefore recovers $I$ and
$Q$ exactly, that is, $z = \mathrm{LP}\{2s(t)e^{-j2\pi f_ct}\}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
The identities are the product formulas $2\cos^2a = 1 + \cos 2a$,
$2\sin a\cos a = \sin 2a$ and $2\sin^2a = 1 - \cos 2a$. Multiplying a signal by
$\cos(4\pi f_ct)$ or $\sin(4\pi f_ct)$ shifts its spectrum up and down by $2f_c$
(@sec-sampling), so the spectra of the extra terms are the bands
$[-W, W] \pm 2f_c$. If $2f_c - W > W$, the band of the wanted terms and those of
the unwanted do not overlap, and an ideal filter separates them. Adding the first
line to $j$ times the second gives $2se^{-j2\pi f_ct}$.
:::

In a radio, the mixer does this in analog circuits and the converter samples $I$
and $Q$. We check the proposition with a scaled-down radio (carrier of 100 kHz,
sampling rate of 800 kHz): an FM signal is built from its complex envelope, mixed
down with a cosine and a sine, filtered, and compared with the original
envelope.

```{python}
fs_r, fc_r = 800_000, 100_000
n_r = np.arange(int(0.05 * fs_r))
t_r = n_r / fs_r
msg = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 1_000 * t_r) + 0.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 2_300 * t_r)      # a two-tone message
z_true = np.exp(1j * 2 * np.pi * 20_000 * np.cumsum(msg) / fs_r)                    # FM, k_f = 20 kHz
s_rf = np.real(z_true * np.exp(2j * np.pi * fc_r * t_r))                            # the radio-frequency signal
lowpass = signal.firwin(255, 60_000, fs=fs_r)                                       # cut-off between W and 2 f_c - W
I = np.convolve(2 * s_rf * np.cos(2 * np.pi * fc_r * t_r), lowpass, mode="same")
Q = np.convolve(-2 * s_rf * np.sin(2 * np.pi * fc_r * t_r), lowpass, mode="same")
z_rec = I + 1j * Q
inner = slice(300, len(t_r) - 300)                                                  # away from the edge effects
err = np.linalg.norm((z_rec - z_true)[inner]) / np.linalg.norm(z_true[inner])
print(f"relative error of the recovered complex envelope: {err:.1e}")
assert err < 5e-3
print(f"samples per second: the radio signal needs {fs_r}, the envelope needs only about {2 * 60_000} (I and Q at ~{60_000} Hz bandwidth)")
```

The envelope is recovered, to the precision of the filter, from the real signal
at the carrier: and its bandwidth is that of the *message* ($60$ kHz here), not
that of the carrier. This is why an SDR delivers I and Q at the rate of the
band, and not of the carrier.

### Recovering the message: the discriminator

The last piece of the theory tells us how to read the message from $z$. For FM
the message is in the angle of $z$, so we need the angle's rate of change. For
samples, the following is exact.

::: {#prp-discriminator}
## The FM discriminator

Let $z[n] = a[n]\,e^{j\phi[n]}$ with $a[n] > 0$ and $|\phi[n] - \phi[n-1]| < \pi$.
Then
$$
\frac{F_s}{2\pi}\arg\big(z[n]\,\overline{z[n-1]}\big) = \frac{F_s}{2\pi}\big(\phi[n] - \phi[n-1]\big),
$$
whatever the amplitudes $a[n]$. If $\phi[n] = 2\pi\sum_{k\le n}f_k/F_s$, the
left-hand side equals $f_n$, the instantaneous frequency in Hz.
:::

::: {.proof}
$z[n]\overline{z[n-1]} = a[n]a[n-1]\,e^{j(\phi[n] - \phi[n-1])}$, a positive number
times a unit complex number whose angle is $\phi[n] - \phi[n-1]$. The principal
value of the angle, $\arg \in (-\pi, \pi]$, equals the difference when the
difference is in that interval. For the second statement,
$\phi[n] - \phi[n-1] = 2\pi f_n/F_s$.
:::

Two consequences matter. First, the FM receiver is **insensitive to the
amplitude**: fading and interference that change $a[n]$ do not affect the
output. Second, the discriminator is one line of code. We check both on the
message of the scaled-down radio:

```{python}
def discriminator(z, rate):
    """Instantaneous frequency (Hz) of a complex signal: (rate / 2 pi) arg(z[n] conj(z[n-1]))."""
    return rate / (2 * np.pi) * np.angle(z[1:] * np.conj(z[:-1]))

freq = discriminator(z_true, fs_r)
assert np.allclose(freq, 20_000 * msg[1:], atol=1e-8)               # exact, @prp-discriminator
fading = 1.0 + 0.8 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 37 * t_r) * rng.uniform(0.5, 1.0, len(t_r))   # an irregular amplitude, always > 0
freq_fading = discriminator(fading * z_true, fs_r)
assert np.allclose(freq_fading, freq, atol=1e-8)                    # the amplitude does not matter
freq_rf = discriminator(z_rec, fs_r)                                # from the mixer's output
print(f"discriminator on the exact envelope: error {np.max(np.abs(freq - 20_000 * msg[1:])):.1e} Hz; "
      f"after the mixer: {np.max(np.abs(freq_rf - 20_000 * msg[1:])[300:-300]):.0f} Hz of a deviation of 20000 Hz")
assert np.max(np.abs(freq_rf - 20_000 * msg[1:])[300:-300]) < 200
```

## The signal of an FM broadcast station {#sec-sdr-broadcast}

### Stereo on a mono radio

A broadcast station sends two audio channels, left $L$ and right $R$, in a way
that a mono receiver, which knows nothing about stereo, can still decode a
good mono signal. It does it with a **composite signal** (or multiplex, MPX)
$m(t)$, which is the message of the FM modulator. With $L$ and $R$ normalised to
$|L|, |R| \le 1$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
m(t) &= 0.9\left[\frac{L(t) + R(t)}{2} + \frac{L(t) - R(t)}{2}\sin(2\pi\,38\,\mathrm{kHz}\;t)\right]\\
&\quad + 0.1\sin(2\pi\,19\,\mathrm{kHz}\;t).
\end{aligned}
$$
The three parts occupy different frequencies:

- $(L + R)/2$, the mono signal, is in the baseband, $0$ to $15$ kHz. A mono receiver
  decodes this and nothing else, and plays the average of the two channels.
- The **pilot**, a tone of 19 kHz at 10 % of the deviation, is a flag that says
  "this is a stereo station", and a phase reference for the receiver.
- $(L - R)/2$ is shifted to 38 kHz (twice the pilot) by multiplying with a
  sinusoid, and occupies $23$ to $53$ kHz. Without a carrier: the product has no
  line at 38 kHz (this is called double-sideband suppressed-carrier modulation),
  and its phase must be reconstructed by the receiver from the pilot.

A stereo receiver recovers $(L + R)/2$ and $(L - R)/2$ and combines them:
$L = \tfrac{L+R}{2} + \tfrac{L-R}{2}$, $R = \tfrac{L+R}{2} - \tfrac{L-R}{2}$. The
normalisation is chosen so that the composite signal does not exceed the deviation.

::: {#prp-composite}
## The composite signal is bounded

If $|L(t)|, |R(t)| \le 1$ then $|m(t)| \le 1$ for the composite signal above.
:::

::: {.proof}
For real $a, b$, $|a + b| + |a - b| = 2\max(|a|, |b|)$ (if $|a| \ge |b|$ both
terms are $|a| \pm |b|$ added: $|a| + |b| + |a| - |b|$). Hence
$\big|\tfrac{L+R}{2}\big| + \big|\tfrac{L-R}{2}\big| = \max(|L|, |R|) \le 1$,
and $|m| \le 0.9\cdot 1 + 0.1 = 1$.
:::

The bound is what guarantees that the carrier never deviates by more than
75 kHz: the modulator uses $k_f = 75$ kHz per unit of $m$.

### Pre-emphasis

There is one more ingredient, which comes from noise. In the receiver, the noise
of an FM demodulator is *not* white: its power density grows with the square of
the frequency (we measure it in the later stages). The audio of music has most
of its energy at low frequencies and much less near 15 kHz, so the high
frequencies are the ones most damaged. The station compensates in advance: it
boosts the high frequencies before modulating, this is **pre-emphasis**, and the
receiver cancels the boost with the inverse filter, **de-emphasis**, which
also lowers the noise at the same frequencies. The time constant of the analog
curve, $\tau = 50\ \mu$s in Europe and $75\ \mu$s in the Americas, corresponds to
a corner at $1/(2\pi\tau) = 3.2$ kHz or $2.1$ kHz [@itu450]. We use a digital
version: the de-emphasis is the one-pole low-pass filter
$y[n] = (1 - a)x[n] + a\,y[n-1]$ with $a = e^{-1/(\tau F_s)}$, and the pre-emphasis
is its inverse, a two-tap FIR filter, which is exact:

```{python}
def pre_emphasis(x, rate, tau=50e-6):
    """Boost of the high frequencies: the inverse of the one-pole de-emphasis, (x[n] - a x[n-1]) / (1 - a)."""
    a = np.exp(-1 / (tau * rate))
    return signal.lfilter([1, -a], [1 - a], x)

def de_emphasis(y, rate, tau=50e-6):
    """One-pole low-pass with the time constant tau: y[n] = (1 - a) x[n] + a y[n - 1]."""
    a = np.exp(-1 / (tau * rate))
    return signal.lfilter([1 - a], [1, -a], y)

x_test = rng.normal(size=5_000)
assert np.allclose(de_emphasis(pre_emphasis(x_test, 48_000), 48_000), x_test, atol=1e-12)   # exact inverses
w_, h_ = signal.freqz([1, -np.exp(-1 / (50e-6 * 48_000))], [1 - np.exp(-1 / (50e-6 * 48_000))], worN=[1e-9, 2 * np.pi * 15_000 / 48_000])
print(f"gain of the pre-emphasis at 15 kHz: {20 * np.log10(abs(h_[1])):.1f} dB "
      f"(the analog curve 1 + j 2 pi f tau gives {20 * np.log10(abs(1 + 2j * np.pi * 15_000 * 50e-6)):.1f} dB)")
assert abs(20 * np.log10(abs(h_[1])) - 20 * np.log10(abs(1 + 2j * np.pi * 15_000 * 50e-6))) < 2
```

### What a station plays: the program material

We need something for the stations to broadcast. To keep the chapter
self-contained we synthesise four short programs by additive synthesis (a few
harmonics with an exponential decay, as in a plucked string, @sec-pedalboard): a
stereo piece with different left and right parts, a mono piece, a stereo chord
sequence and a second mono piece. Their sound is not important; they are different
from one another, and the stereo ones have $L \ne R$, so that the receiver can
show that it reconstructs the stereo image.

```{python}
fs_audio, fs_mpx, fs_rf = 48_000, 240_000, 960_000             # audio, composite/modulator, tuner output (Hz)
DURATION = 1.5                                                # seconds of capture

def tone(f, dur, rate, decay=5.0):
    """A plucked-like tone: four harmonics with an exponential decay and a soft attack."""
    t = np.arange(int(dur * rate)) / rate
    y = sum(a * np.sin(2 * np.pi * k * f * t) for k, a in enumerate((1.0, 0.5, 0.25, 0.12), start=1))
    return y * np.exp(-decay * t) * (1 - np.exp(-300 * t))

def track(notes, step, rate=fs_audio, dur=DURATION, decay=5.0):
    """Notes given as (frequency in Hz, start in steps): a sequence of tones at a regular step in seconds."""
    out = np.zeros(int(dur * rate))
    for f, k in notes:
        y = tone(f, 0.6, rate, decay)
        i = int(k * step * rate)
        out[i:i + len(y)] += y[:len(out) - i]
    return out

def program(name):
    """The left and right channels of each station's programme, normalised to a peak of 0.9."""
    scale = {"C4": 261.63, "E4": 329.63, "G4": 392.0, "A3": 220.0, "D4": 293.66, "F3": 174.61, "C3": 130.81, "B3": 246.94, "A4": 440.0}
    if name == "A":                                            # stereo: a melody on the left, a bass on the right
        L = track([(scale[n], k) for k, n in enumerate(["C4", "E4", "G4", "E4", "A4", "G4", "E4", "C4"])], 0.18)
        R = track([(scale[n], k) for k, n in zip((0, 4), ["C3", "F3"])], 0.36, decay=3.0)
    elif name == "B":                                          # mono: two alternating tones
        L = R = track([(scale["A4"] if k % 2 else scale["D4"], k) for k in range(8)], 0.18, decay=7.0)
    elif name == "C":                                          # stereo: the notes of a chord spread over the channels
        L = track([(scale["C4"], 0), (scale["G4"], 2), (scale["C4"], 4)], 0.3, decay=3.0)
        R = track([(scale["E4"], 1), (scale["B3"], 3), (scale["E4"], 5)], 0.3, decay=3.0)
    else:                                                      # D: mono, a slow descending line
        L = R = track([(scale[n], k) for k, n in enumerate(["G4", "E4", "D4", "A3"])], 0.35, decay=4.0)
    peak = max(np.max(np.abs(L)), np.max(np.abs(R)))
    return 0.9 * L / peak, 0.9 * R / peak

PROGRAMS = {name: program(name) for name in "ABCD"}
for name, (L, R) in PROGRAMS.items():
    print(f"station {name}: {'stereo' if not np.allclose(L, R) else 'mono  '}  peak {max(np.max(np.abs(L)), np.max(np.abs(R))):.2f}")
assert not np.allclose(*PROGRAMS["A"]) and not np.allclose(*PROGRAMS["C"])
assert np.allclose(*PROGRAMS["B"]) and np.allclose(*PROGRAMS["D"])
```

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
```{python}
Clips({f"Station {name} ({'stereo' if not np.allclose(*PROGRAMS[name]) else 'mono'})": np.column_stack(PROGRAMS[name])
       for name in "ABCD"}, fs_audio)
```
:::

### Building the composite signal

The station applies the pre-emphasis, limits the peaks (we simply normalise
them), and builds the composite signal at a rate high enough to hold it: 240 kHz,
five times the audio rate. The sine at 38 kHz is $\sin(2\theta)$ for the pilot
$\sin(\theta)$, $\theta = 2\pi\,19\,\mathrm{kHz}\;t$: the subcarrier is locked
to the pilot, which is what lets the receiver reconstruct it.

```{python}
def composite(L, R, stereo=True, tau=50e-6):
    """The composite (MPX) signal at fs_mpx, with peak at most 1, from audio channels at fs_audio."""
    Lp, Rp = pre_emphasis(L, fs_audio, tau), pre_emphasis(R, fs_audio, tau)
    peak = max(np.max(np.abs(Lp)), np.max(np.abs(Rp)))
    Lp, Rp = Lp / peak, Rp / peak                              # a limiter: |L|, |R| <= 1 for @prp-composite
    L5, R5 = signal.resample_poly(Lp, 5, 1), signal.resample_poly(Rp, 5, 1)
    theta = 2 * np.pi * 19_000 * np.arange(len(L5)) / fs_mpx
    if not stereo:
        return (L5 + R5) / 2                                   # mono station: no pilot, no subcarrier
    return 0.9 * ((L5 + R5) / 2 + (L5 - R5) / 2 * np.sin(2 * theta)) + 0.1 * np.sin(theta)

MPX = {name: composite(*PROGRAMS[name], stereo=name in "AC") for name in "ABCD"}
for name, m in MPX.items():
    print(f"station {name}: composite peak {np.max(np.abs(m)):.3f}")
    assert np.max(np.abs(m)) <= 1.0 + 0.05                      # @prp-composite (the interpolation filter may overshoot)
```

@fig-mpx shows the composite signal of a stereo station and a mono one. The
stereo station has the structure described: mono baseband, pilot, and the
shifted difference signal around 38 kHz.

```{python}
#| label: fig-mpx
#| fig-cap: "Power spectral density of the composite signal of a stereo station (A, blue) and a mono station (B, orange). Stereo: the mono sum $(L+R)/2$ up to 15 kHz, the pilot at 19 kHz and the difference signal $(L-R)/2$ around 38 kHz; the mono station has only the baseband."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))
for name, colour in (("A", "C0"), ("B", "C1")):
    f, P = welch_psd(MPX[name], fs_mpx, 8192)
    ax.plot(f / 1e3, 10 * np.log10(P + 1e-20), color=colour, lw=0.8, label=f"station {name}")
ax.set(xlim=(0, 60), ylim=(-130, -30), xlabel="frequency [kHz]", ylabel="PSD [dB]")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

fa, Pa = welch_psd(MPX["A"], fs_mpx, 8192)
fb, Pb = welch_psd(MPX["B"], fs_mpx, 8192)
band = lambda f, P, lo, hi: P[(f >= lo) & (f <= hi)].sum()
pilot_a, pilot_b = band(fa, Pa, 18.5e3, 19.5e3), band(fb, Pb, 18.5e3, 19.5e3)
diff_a, diff_b = band(fa, Pa, 23e3, 53e3), band(fb, Pb, 23e3, 53e3)
print(f"pilot power, stereo / mono station: {10 * np.log10(pilot_a / pilot_b):.0f} dB;  "
      f"difference band: {10 * np.log10(diff_a / diff_b):.0f} dB")
assert pilot_a / pilot_b > 1e3 and diff_a / diff_b > 10        # the mono station has neither
```

## Stage 1: the antenna {#sec-sdr-antenna}

### Modulating the carrier

Each station's composite signal is the message of an FM modulator with
$k_f = 75$ kHz. We work with the complex envelope $z[n] = e^{j\varphi[n]}$ at
240 kHz (@sec-sdr-iq): its bandwidth is 180 kHz, so the rate is sufficient. Then
we raise the rate to the 960 kHz of the tuner's output, with a polyphase
interpolator (@sec-multirate), and shift the station to its place in the band by
multiplying by a complex exponential (@sec-complex-numbers): this does the work
of the carrier, since in the envelope the station's frequency relative to the
centre of the tuned band is all that remains.

```{python}
def fm_modulate(m, rate, deviation=75e3):
    """Complex envelope of an FM signal: z[n] = exp(j 2 pi k_f sum(m) / rate); unit modulus."""
    return np.exp(2j * np.pi * deviation * np.cumsum(m) / rate)

def station_signal(m, offset):
    """The FM complex envelope of a station, at the tuner's output rate fs_rf and `offset` Hz from the tuner centre."""
    z = signal.resample_poly(fm_modulate(m, fs_mpx), fs_rf // fs_mpx, 1)
    return z * np.exp(2j * np.pi * offset * np.arange(len(z)) / fs_rf)

# Carrier offsets from the centre of the tuned band (the tuner is set at 98.3 MHz): 98.0, 98.2, 98.4, 98.6 MHz.
STATIONS = {"A": -300e3, "B": -100e3, "C": +100e3, "D": +300e3}
AMPLITUDE = {"A": 1.0, "B": 0.5, "C": 0.8, "D": 0.12}         # received amplitude: D is a faint, far station
signals = {name: station_signal(MPX[name], STATIONS[name]) for name in "ABCD"}
assert all(len(s) == len(signals["A"]) for s in signals.values())
ripple = {name: np.std(np.abs(s)[2000:-2000]) for name, s in signals.items()}   # modulus should be 1 (constant envelope)
print("standard deviation of the modulus (ripple of the interpolation filter):",
      {name: round(float(r), 4) for name, r in ripple.items()})
assert all(r < 0.01 for r in ripple.values())                                    # constant, up to a small ripple
print(f"{len(signals['A'])} complex samples per station ({len(signals['A']) / fs_rf:.2f} s at {fs_rf / 1e3:.0f} kS/s)")
```

### The analog world and the converter

The antenna adds all the stations in the air, together with the noise of the
amplifier. The tuner's oscillator is never exactly at the frequency it is set to
(its quartz has a tolerance of some parts per million): at 98.3 MHz, 25 ppm is
2.5 kHz, so every station appears 2.5 kHz away from where it should be, and the
receiver will have to find out. Finally the converter rounds I and Q to 8 bits,
with a range adjusted by an automatic gain control. We store the result as
interleaved unsigned bytes, *I Q I Q ...*, with the value 127.5 as the zero:
the format of the cheap USB dongles.

```{python}
def analog_band(rng, cnr_db=35.0, lo_error=2.5e3):
    """The band as the mixer delivers it, before the converter: the stations plus noise, shifted by the oscillator's error.

    cnr_db is the carrier-to-noise ratio of the strongest station in its 200 kHz channel."""
    band_sum = sum(AMPLITUDE[name] * signals[name] for name in "ABCD")
    n = len(band_sum)
    noise_var = AMPLITUDE["A"] ** 2 / (10 ** (cnr_db / 10)) * (fs_rf / 200e3)      # per complex sample
    noise = np.sqrt(noise_var / 2) * (rng.normal(size=n) + 1j * rng.normal(size=n))
    return (band_sum + noise) * np.exp(2j * np.pi * lo_error * np.arange(n) / fs_rf)  # the oscillator's error

def quantise_iq(x, bits=8):
    """The converter: interleaved unsigned bytes I Q I Q ... with an automatic gain control."""
    full_scale = 3.5 * np.sqrt(np.mean(np.abs(x) ** 2) / 2)                          # automatic gain control
    levels = 2 ** bits - 1
    to_byte = lambda v: np.clip(np.round((v / full_scale + 1) / 2 * levels), 0, levels).astype(np.uint8)
    raw = np.empty(2 * len(x), dtype=np.uint8)
    raw[0::2], raw[1::2] = to_byte(x.real), to_byte(x.imag)
    return raw

def capture(rng, cnr_db=35.0, lo_error=2.5e3, bits=8):
    """What an SDR delivers: unsigned bytes I Q I Q ... of the sum of the stations plus noise."""
    return quantise_iq(analog_band(rng, cnr_db, lo_error), bits)

def bytes_to_iq(raw, bits=8):
    """Interleaved unsigned bytes back to complex samples in [-1, 1]."""
    levels = 2 ** bits - 1
    return ((raw[0::2].astype(float) - levels / 2) + 1j * (raw[1::2].astype(float) - levels / 2)) / (levels / 2)

raw = capture(np.random.default_rng(88))
iq = bytes_to_iq(raw)
clipped = np.mean((raw == 0) | (raw == 255))
print(f"capture: {len(raw)} bytes = {len(iq)} complex samples; samples at full scale: {100 * clipped:.4f} %")
assert raw.dtype == np.uint8 and len(iq) == len(signals["A"])
assert clipped < 1e-3
```

### Looking at the result

Our first view of the capture is its **power spectral density** (@sec-spectral-analysis).
@fig-capture-psd is what a spectrum-analyser program shows when it is connected to an
SDR: four bumps, each about 180 kHz wide, over a flat noise floor, the faint
station D barely above it.

```{python}
#| label: fig-capture-psd
#| fig-cap: "Power spectral density of the 8-bit capture, relative to the tuner's centre. The four bumps are the stations A to D, 200 kHz apart; the whole picture is shifted 2.5 kHz by the error of the tuner's oscillator. The dashed lines mark the nominal positions."
f_cap, P_cap = psd_db(iq, fs_rf)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))
ax.plot(f_cap / 1e3, P_cap, lw=0.7)
for name, off in STATIONS.items():
    ax.axvline(off / 1e3, color="C3", ls="--", lw=0.6)
    ax.text(off / 1e3, P_cap.max() + 2, name, ha="center", color="C3", fontsize=9)
ax.set(xlabel="frequency from the tuner centre [kHz]", ylabel="PSD [dB]", ylim=(P_cap.min() - 3, P_cap.max() + 8))
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

floor_mask = (np.abs(f_cap) > 410e3) & (np.abs(f_cap) < 470e3)                 # outside every channel
floor_lin = np.mean(10 ** (P_cap[floor_mask] / 10))                              # noise density, flat
df = f_cap[1] - f_cap[0]
power = {}
for name, off in STATIONS.items():
    inside = np.abs(f_cap - off - 2.5e3) < 95e3                                  # the 200 kHz channel, almost
    power[name] = np.sum(10 ** (P_cap[inside] / 10)) * df - floor_lin * inside.sum() * df   # signal power, noise removed
print(f"{'station':>8} {'level above the floor':>22} {'power relative to A':>20} {'amplitude chosen':>17}")
for name in "ABCD":
    above = 10 * np.log10(np.mean(10 ** (P_cap[np.abs(f_cap - STATIONS[name] - 2.5e3) < 80e3] / 10)) / floor_lin)
    ratio = 10 * np.log10(power[name] / power["A"])
    expected = 20 * np.log10(AMPLITUDE[name] / AMPLITUDE["A"])
    print(f"{name:>8} {above:19.1f} dB {ratio:17.1f} dB {expected:14.1f} dB")
    assert above > 10                                                            # all four stand out of the noise
    assert abs(ratio - expected) < 1.0                                           # the power is the amplitude squared
```

The power measured in each channel follows the amplitudes that we chose for the
stations (the power of a constant-envelope signal is the square of its amplitude, and
the spectrum is only the way it is spread: a stereo station occupies more bandwidth
than a mono one, so its density is lower for the same power). We have
reached the place where a real receiver starts: an array of complex samples
from an antenna and a converter, and nothing else. The rest of the project
takes it from here to a pair of loudspeakers.

## Stage 2: looking at the band {#sec-sdr-spectrum}

A receiver must first find out what is on the air. A real one does what you do
when you scan the dial: it measures the power in every channel where a station
could be. FM channels are on a regular grid, 200 kHz apart, so the receiver
only has to look at a few candidate **channels**, and to call a channel occupied
when its power is well above the noise floor. The floor is measured where
there is probably no station: the quietest 100 kHz of the captured band (a crowded
band has stations at its edges, so the edges are not a safe place to look).

A second question is where *exactly* the carrier is, because the tuner's
oscillator is not exact. A music signal modulated in frequency has a spectrum
that is, on average, symmetric around the carrier, so we estimate the carrier
as the **centroid** of the power inside the channel: the average of the
frequencies weighted by the power above the noise floor. Since a centroid
computed in a window that is not centred on the carrier is biased, the estimate is
repeated three times, each one centring the window on the previous result.

```{python}
CHANNELS = np.arange(-300e3, 300e3 + 1, 200e3)                 # the 200 kHz grid, as offsets from the tuner centre

def scan_channels(f, P_db, centres=CHANNELS, half=90e3, margin_db=10.0):
    """Dial scan on a PSD (in dB). Returns [(carrier offset in Hz, carrier-to-noise ratio in dB), ...]
    for the channels whose power is at least margin_db above the noise floor."""
    P = 10 ** (P_db / 10)
    df = f[1] - f[0]
    n_quiet = int(100e3 / df)
    floor = np.convolve(P, np.ones(n_quiet) / n_quiet, mode="valid").min()   # noise density: the quietest 100 kHz
    found = []
    for c in centres:
        window = np.abs(f - c) < half
        cnr = np.sum(P[window] - floor) * df / (floor * 2 * half)         # signal power / noise power in the window
        if 10 * np.log10(max(cnr, 1e-9)) > margin_db:
            for _ in range(3):                                           # centroid, re-centred three times
                window = np.abs(f - c) < half
                c = np.sum(f[window] * (P[window] - floor)) / np.sum(P[window] - floor)
            found.append((c, 10 * np.log10(cnr)))
    return found

f_cap, P_cap = psd_db(iq, fs_rf)
found = scan_channels(f_cap, P_cap)
true_carriers = {name: STATIONS[name] + 2.5e3 for name in "ABCD"}      # where the stations really are (tuner error included)
print(f"{'station':>8} {'estimated carrier':>18} {'true carrier':>14} {'error':>8} {'CNR in 180 kHz':>15}")
for (c, cnr), name in zip(found, "ABCD"):
    print(f"{name:>8} {c / 1e3:15.2f} kHz {true_carriers[name] / 1e3:11.2f} kHz {c - true_carriers[name]:5.0f} Hz {cnr:12.1f} dB")
assert len(found) == 4                                                  # the four stations, and no other channel
assert all(abs(c - true_carriers[name]) < 300 for (c, _), name in zip(found, "ABCD"))
tuner_error = np.mean([c - STATIONS[name] for (c, _), name in zip(found, "ABCD")])
print(f"the receiver has measured the tuner's error: {tuner_error:.0f} Hz")
assert abs(tuner_error - 2.5e3) < 200
```

The receiver finds the four stations, rejects the empty channels, and measures the
oscillator error (2.5 kHz) from the stations themselves. The faint station D is
found too: it is much weaker than A, but still well above the noise.

## Stage 3: tuning {#sec-sdr-tuning}

To work on one station we move it to zero frequency: multiplying the samples by
a complex exponential shifts the whole spectrum. In the complex envelope this is
exact, with no image to filter out, and it costs one complex multiplication
per sample.

::: {#prp-shift}
## The frequency shift

Let $X(e^{j\omega})$ be the DTFT of $x[n]$. The DTFT of $y[n] = x[n]e^{-j\omega_0n}$
is $Y(e^{j\omega}) = X(e^{j(\omega + \omega_0)})$: the spectrum moves by $-\omega_0$ (modulo
$2\pi$). In Hz, multiplying by $e^{-j2\pi f_0n/F_s}$ moves the spectrum by $-f_0$.
:::

::: {.proof}
$Y(e^{j\omega}) = \sum_nx[n]e^{-j\omega_0n}e^{-j\omega n} = \sum_nx[n]e^{-j(\omega + \omega_0)n}$,
which is $X$ evaluated at $\omega + \omega_0$ (@sec-spectral-analysis).
:::

```{python}
def tune(x, f_offset, rate):
    """Move the spectrum of x down by f_offset Hz (a complex mixer)."""
    return x * np.exp(-2j * np.pi * f_offset * np.arange(len(x)) / rate)

def centroid(f, P_db, centre, half=90e3):
    P = 10 ** (P_db / 10)
    window = np.abs(f - centre) < half
    return np.sum(f[window] * P[window]) / np.sum(P[window])

carriers = [c for c, _ in found]
for name, c in zip("ABCD", carriers):
    f_t, P_t = psd_db(tune(iq, c, fs_rf), fs_rf)
    cen = centroid(f_t, P_t, 0.0)
    print(f"station {name}: after tuning, the centroid of its channel is at {cen:7.1f} Hz")
    assert abs(cen) < 600                                       # the station is now at zero frequency
```

## Stage 4: selecting the channel {#sec-sdr-channel}

After tuning, the station is at zero frequency, and the neighbours are
200 kHz above and below it. The capture is at 960 kS/s but a single station is
only 180 kHz wide, so we want to reduce the rate to 240 kS/s (a factor of 4),
which makes everything that follows four times cheaper. Decimation is not
discarding three samples out of four: that would fold everything from 120 kHz up
into the band we keep (@sec-multirate), including the neighbours, whose
spectrum is at $\pm200$ kHz and would land at $\mp40$ kHz, on top of our station.
The signal must be filtered first, with a **channel filter**. The specification
follows from the signal:

- the passband must carry the station: $\pm90$ kHz (Carson's band, 180 kHz);
- the stopband must start where the neighbouring station can begin: it is
  centred 200 kHz away and extends to $\pm90$ kHz around it, so it starts at
  $200 - 90 = 110$ kHz;
- the rejection must be well above the difference in strength between stations,
  which here reaches 18 dB; we ask for 60 dB.

This is a low-pass FIR filter with a transition band of 20 kHz at a sampling
rate of 960 kHz, and attenuation of 60 dB: a **Kaiser window** design
(@sec-filter-design). The filter has linear phase, so it delays the signal by
exactly $(N - 1)/2$ samples, and we compensate it. We implement the filter and
the decimation together with a polyphase structure (`upfirdn`), which computes only the
output samples that are kept: one output of $N$ multiplications every four
input samples, and not four.

```{python}
#| label: fig-channel-filter
#| fig-cap: "The channel filter (red) over the spectrum of the capture tuned to station A (blue). It passes the station (|f| < 90 kHz) and removes the neighbours, which start at 110 kHz, by more than 60 dB. Right: after decimation by 4 with the filter the spectrum is clean (blue); without it, by keeping every fourth sample, the neighbours fold on top of the station (orange)."
def channel_filter(passband=90e3, stopband=110e3, atten=60.0, rate=fs_rf):
    """Kaiser-window low-pass FIR with the given band edges (Hz) and stopband attenuation (dB)."""
    n_taps, beta = signal.kaiserord(atten, (stopband - passband) / (rate / 2))
    n_taps += 1 - n_taps % 2                                      # odd length: integer delay
    return signal.firwin(n_taps, (passband + stopband) / 2, window=("kaiser", beta), fs=rate)

def select_channel(x, f_offset, h, down=4):
    """Tune to f_offset, filter with h and decimate by `down` (polyphase), compensating the filter's delay."""
    y = signal.upfirdn(h, tune(x, f_offset, fs_rf), up=1, down=down)
    return y[(len(h) - 1) // 2 // down:]

h_ch = channel_filter()
w_h, H_h = signal.freqz(h_ch, worN=8192, fs=fs_rf)
stop = w_h >= 110e3
print(f"channel filter: {len(h_ch)} taps; attenuation beyond 110 kHz: {-20 * np.log10(np.abs(H_h[stop]).max()):.1f} dB; "
      f"passband ripple: {np.abs(20 * np.log10(np.abs(H_h[w_h <= 90e3]))).max():.3f} dB")
assert -20 * np.log10(np.abs(H_h[stop]).max()) >= 59.5
assert np.abs(20 * np.log10(np.abs(H_h[w_h <= 90e3]))).max() < 0.05
assert (len(h_ch) - 1) // 2 % 4 == 0                            # the delay is a whole number of output samples

tuned_A = tune(iq, carriers[0], fs_rf)
f_a, P_a = psd_db(tuned_A, fs_rf)
x_sel = select_channel(iq, carriers[0], h_ch)                    # filtered, 240 kS/s
x_naive = tuned_A[::4]                                          # every fourth sample, no filter
f_s, P_s = psd_db(x_sel, fs_mpx, nperseg=1024)
f_n, P_n = psd_db(x_naive, fs_mpx, nperseg=1024)

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.4, 3), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.3, 1]})
ax1.plot(f_a / 1e3, P_a, lw=0.6)
ax1.plot(w_h / 1e3, 20 * np.log10(np.abs(H_h) + 1e-9) + P_a.max() - 10, "C3", lw=0.9)
ax1.plot(-w_h / 1e3, 20 * np.log10(np.abs(H_h) + 1e-9) + P_a.max() - 10, "C3", lw=0.9)
ax1.set(xlabel="frequency [kHz]", ylabel="PSD [dB]", title="960 kS/s: tuned, with the filter", ylim=(P_a.min() - 3, P_a.max() + 5))
ax2.plot(f_n / 1e3, P_n, color="C1", lw=0.7, label="no filter")
ax2.plot(f_s / 1e3, P_s, color="C0", lw=0.9, label="with the filter")
ax2.set(xlabel="frequency [kHz]", title="240 kS/s", ylim=(P_s.min() - 3, P_n.max() + 5))
ax2.legend(fontsize=7)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

To measure how well the filter isolates a station we use the linearity of the
whole process. The capture is the sum of the stations (plus noise); what comes out
of the filter for the sum is the sum of what comes out for each station. So we
pass each station *alone* through the tuning, the filter and the decimation, and
compare the power that comes from the wanted station with the power that comes
from all the others. We do the same for the naive decimation.

```{python}
def station_in_air(name):
    """The (noise-free) contribution of one station to the capture, as the antenna would deliver it."""
    return AMPLITUDE[name] * signals[name] * np.exp(2j * np.pi * 2.5e3 * np.arange(len(signals[name])) / fs_rf)

def adjacent_channel_ratio_db(wanted, method):
    """Power of the wanted station over the power of the others at the output of `method`, in dB."""
    carrier = true_carriers[wanted]
    own = method(station_in_air(wanted), carrier)
    others = sum(method(station_in_air(n), carrier) for n in "ABCD" if n != wanted)
    n = min(len(own), len(others))
    return 10 * np.log10(np.sum(np.abs(own[:n]) ** 2) / np.sum(np.abs(others[:n]) ** 2))

with_filter = lambda x, c: select_channel(x, c, h_ch)
without_filter = lambda x, c: tune(x, c, fs_rf)[::4]
print(f"{'station':>8} {'with the filter':>17} {'every 4th sample':>18}")
for name in "AC":
    r_f, r_n = adjacent_channel_ratio_db(name, with_filter), adjacent_channel_ratio_db(name, without_filter)
    print(f"{name:>8} {r_f:14.1f} dB {r_n:15.1f} dB")
    assert r_f > 55                                              # the neighbours are suppressed ...
    assert r_n < 10                                              # ... and, without the filter, they are as strong as the station
```

With the filter, the neighbours *all together* are more than 55 dB below the station.
Without it, their power is of the order of the station's own, and the rest of the
receiver would hear them.

## Stage 5: demodulation {#sec-sdr-demod}

Now the discriminator of @prp-discriminator does its job. Its output
is the instantaneous frequency in Hz; dividing by the deviation of
75 kHz gives the composite signal $m$, scaled to the range $[-1, 1]$ of the
transmitter. Because the tuner and the oscillator of the station are not exactly
in tune, the frequency has a constant offset, which becomes a constant added to
$m$ (a DC component): with the centroid estimate from Stage 2 the error is small
and can be measured as the mean of the output, and removed. This is the
simplest **automatic frequency control**.

```{python}
def demodulate(x, rate=fs_mpx, deviation=75e3):
    """FM demodulation: the discriminator output in units of the deviation, and its mean (the residual offset in Hz)."""
    m = discriminator(x, rate) / deviation
    return m - np.mean(m), np.mean(m) * deviation

m_hat, residual = demodulate(x_sel)
print(f"residual frequency error after the tuning of Stage 2: {residual:.1f} Hz (the offset to start with: 2500 Hz)")
assert abs(residual) < 100

def align_lag(est, ref, max_lag=2000):
    """The delay of est with respect to ref in samples, from the peak of their cross-correlation (@sec-signals-as-vectors)."""
    n = min(len(est), len(ref))
    X = np.fft.rfft(est[:n] - np.mean(est[:n]), 2 * n)
    Y = np.fft.rfft(ref[:n] - np.mean(ref[:n]), 2 * n)
    cc = np.fft.irfft(X * np.conj(Y))
    cc = np.r_[cc[-max_lag:], cc[:max_lag + 1]]
    return int(np.argmax(np.abs(cc))) - max_lag

def fit_snr_db(est, ref, skip=0, lag=None):
    """SNR of est against ref, after aligning them and scaling ref by the least-squares gain."""
    lag = align_lag(est, ref) if lag is None else lag
    if lag >= 0:
        est = est[lag:]
    else:
        ref = ref[-lag:]
    n = min(len(est), len(ref))
    e, r = est[skip:n], ref[skip:n]
    g = np.dot(e, r) / np.dot(r, r)
    return 10 * np.log10(np.sum((g * r) ** 2) / np.sum((e - g * r) ** 2)), lag, g

snr_c, lag_c, gain_c = fit_snr_db(m_hat, MPX["A"], skip=2000)
print(f"composite signal of station A: SNR {snr_c:.1f} dB against what the station sent (delay {lag_c} samples, gain {gain_c:.3f})")
assert snr_c > 20 and abs(gain_c - 1) < 0.01                      # the gain is 1: the deviation was recovered correctly
```

@fig-composite-rx shows the spectrum of the demodulated composite signal of a stereo station
and of a mono one: the structure of @fig-mpx has come back from the antenna,
now on top of a floor that grows with frequency.

```{python}
#| label: fig-composite-rx
#| fig-cap: "Power spectral density of the composite signal recovered by the receiver for station A (stereo, blue) and station B (mono, orange). The mono sum, the pilot at 19 kHz and the difference signal around 38 kHz of the stereo station are there; beyond 60 kHz there is only noise, which rises with frequency (this is the noise of an FM discriminator)."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))
m_hat_B, _ = demodulate(select_channel(iq, carriers[1], h_ch))
for name, m_rx, colour in (("A", m_hat, "C0"), ("B", m_hat_B, "C1")):
    f, P = welch_psd(m_rx, fs_mpx, 8192)
    ax.plot(f / 1e3, 10 * np.log10(P + 1e-20), color=colour, lw=0.8, label=f"station {name}")
ax.set(xlim=(0, 110), ylim=(-100, -20), xlabel="frequency [kHz]", ylabel="PSD [dB]")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Stage 6: stereo decoding {#sec-sdr-stereo}

The receiver has the composite signal and must now undo the multiplex of
@sec-sdr-broadcast. First, it must decide whether the station is stereo: is
there a pilot? The pilot is a line at 19 kHz, so we compare the power there
with the power in two quiet bands next to it.

```{python}
def pilot_level_db(m, rate=fs_mpx):
    """Power around 19 kHz relative to the power at 17-18 kHz and 20-21 kHz, in dB."""
    f, P = welch_psd(m, rate, 8192)
    near = P[(f > 18.9e3) & (f < 19.1e3)].mean()
    around = P[((f > 17e3) & (f < 18e3)) | ((f > 20e3) & (f < 21e3))].mean()
    return 10 * np.log10(near / around)

levels = {}
for name, c in zip("ABCD", carriers):
    levels[name] = pilot_level_db(demodulate(select_channel(iq, c, h_ch))[0])
    print(f"station {name}: pilot {levels[name]:5.1f} dB above its surroundings -> {'stereo' if levels[name] > 15 else 'mono'}")
assert levels["A"] > 15 and levels["C"] > 15 and levels["B"] < 6 and levels["D"] < 6
```

A **mono** station (or a stereo one that we decode as mono) needs only the
baseband: a low-pass filter of 15 kHz that removes the pilot and the difference
signal gives $0.9(L + R)/2$. For stereo we need $(L - R)/2$, which is
$\sin(2\pi\,38\,\mathrm{kHz}\,t)$ times the signal. To undo a multiplication by
a sinusoid we multiply by the same sinusoid, **in phase** with the one that
the station used. We have a way of knowing the phase: the pilot. Its frequency
is half that of the subcarrier and the station keeps them locked.

### The phase-locked loop

We recover the phase of the pilot with a **phase-locked loop** (PLL), the same
device that synchronised the carrier of the modem in @sec-modem-sync. A local
oscillator (an NCO) produces a sine with phase $\hat\theta[n]$. A *phase
detector* multiplies it by the received pilot: since
$\sin\theta\cos\hat\theta = \tfrac12[\sin(\theta - \hat\theta) + \sin(\theta + \hat\theta)]$,
the product contains a term $\tfrac12\sin(\theta - \hat\theta)$, proportional to the
phase error, plus a term at 38 kHz that the loop's own lag smooths away. A
*loop filter* of proportional and integral action turns the error into a correction
of the oscillator's frequency, and the oscillator accumulates it:
$$
\begin{aligned}
e[n] &= p[n]\cos\hat\theta[n],\\
\hat\theta[n+1] &= \hat\theta[n] + \omega_0 + k_pe[n] + s[n],\\
s[n] &= s[n-1] + k_ie[n],
\end{aligned}
$$
where $\omega_0 = 2\pi\cdot19\,\mathrm{kHz}/F_s$ is the nominal frequency and $s$ is
the integrator, which learns the small deviation between the oscillator and the
pilot. When the loop is locked, $\theta - \hat\theta \approx 0$ and
$\sin(2\hat\theta)$ is the subcarrier. The gains follow from the loop's natural
frequency $\omega_n$ and damping $\zeta$ (we take $\zeta = 0.707$ and a bandwidth
of 50 Hz), for a detector gain $K_d = A_p/2$ with $A_p$ the amplitude of the pilot:
$k_p = 2\zeta\omega_n/K_d$, $k_i = \omega_n^2/K_d$.

```{python}
#| label: fig-pll
#| fig-cap: "The phase-locked loop acquiring the pilot of station A. Top: the phase detector's output $e[n]$ (blue) and its average over 1 ms (orange); the loop locks in the first milliseconds and then the average is zero. Bottom: the frequency that the loop's integrator has learned, which settles at the pilot's offset from the nominal 19 kHz."
def pilot_pll(p, rate=fs_mpx, f0=19e3, bandwidth=50.0, zeta=0.707):
    """Second-order phase-locked loop on a real pilot p = A sin(theta). Returns theta_hat[n], e[n], s[n]."""
    omega_n = 2 * np.pi * bandwidth / rate
    amplitude = np.sqrt(2 * np.mean(p ** 2))
    k_d = amplitude / 2
    k_p, k_i = 2 * zeta * omega_n / k_d, omega_n ** 2 / k_d
    w0 = 2 * np.pi * f0 / rate
    theta, integrator = 0.0, 0.0
    th, err, freq = np.empty(len(p)), np.empty(len(p)), np.empty(len(p))
    for n in range(len(p)):
        th[n] = theta
        e = p[n] * np.cos(theta)                             # the phase detector
        integrator += k_i * e
        theta += w0 + k_p * e + integrator
        err[n], freq[n] = e, integrator
    return th, err, freq

def extract_pilot(m, rate=fs_mpx):
    """The pilot: a band-pass FIR filter around 19 kHz (zero delay: the convolution is centred)."""
    return np.convolve(m, signal.firwin(401, [18.5e3, 19.5e3], pass_zero=False, fs=rate), mode="same")

pilot_A = extract_pilot(m_hat)
theta_A, err_A, freq_A = pilot_pll(pilot_A)
t_ms = np.arange(len(err_A)) / fs_mpx * 1e3
avg = np.convolve(err_A, np.ones(240) / 240, mode="same")                         # 1 ms average
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(7, 3.8), sharex=True)
ax1.plot(t_ms[:6000], err_A[:6000], lw=0.4, label="$e[n]$")
ax1.plot(t_ms[:6000], avg[:6000], lw=1.2, label="1 ms average")
ax1.set(ylabel="phase detector"); ax1.legend(fontsize=7)
ax2.plot(t_ms[:6000], freq_A[:6000] * fs_mpx / (2 * np.pi), lw=1)
ax2.set(xlabel="time [ms]", ylabel="learned offset [Hz]")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

locked = np.abs(avg[24000:]).max()                                                 # after 0.1 s
print(f"phase detector, averaged over 1 ms, after 0.1 s: at most {locked:.2e}  (pilot amplitude {np.sqrt(2 * np.mean(pilot_A ** 2)):.3f})")
assert locked < 0.1 * np.sqrt(2 * np.mean(pilot_A ** 2)) / 2          # a tenth of the detector's full range
```

### Decoding the difference signal

With the subcarrier $\sin(2\hat\theta)$ we multiply the composite signal by it and
low-pass filter: the product of $\tfrac{L-R}{2}\sin(2\theta)$ by $2\sin(2\hat\theta)$ is
$\tfrac{L-R}{2}[1 - \cos(4\theta)]$, whose first term is the baseband
signal we want and the second one is at 76 kHz and is removed by the filter. The
matrix then gives the channels, as in @sec-sdr-broadcast. How important is the
phase of the subcarrier?

::: {#prp-stereo-phase}
## Stereo separation against the phase error

Let the receiver regenerate the subcarrier with a phase error $\varepsilon$,
$\sin(2\theta + \varepsilon)$ instead of $\sin(2\theta)$, and let $M = (L + R)/2$ and
$D = (L - R)/2$. Then the decoded signals are $M$ and $D\cos\varepsilon$ (apart from
the low-pass filtering and the scale), and
$$
\hat L = M + D\cos\varepsilon = \frac{1 + \cos\varepsilon}{2}\,L + \frac{1 - \cos\varepsilon}{2}\,R .
$$
Crosstalk: the right channel appears in the left output with the relative
amplitude $\dfrac{1 - \cos\varepsilon}{1 + \cos\varepsilon} = \tan^2(\varepsilon/2)$.
:::

::: {.proof}
$2\sin(2\theta + \varepsilon)\sin(2\theta) = \cos\varepsilon - \cos(4\theta + \varepsilon)$, and the low-pass filter keeps
$\cos\varepsilon$ times $D$. Then $M + D\cos\varepsilon$ gives the formula, because
$M = (L + R)/2$ and $D = (L - R)/2$. The ratio of the coefficients is
$(1 - \cos\varepsilon)/(1 + \cos\varepsilon) = \tan^2(\varepsilon/2)$ by the half-angle identities.
:::

The loop keeps $\varepsilon$ almost zero, but the proposition shows why it is needed:
a phase error of $15°$, small to the eye, leaves a separation of 35 dB, one of $60°$
only 9.5 dB. We implement the decoder and test the proposition by deliberately
adding an error to the subcarrier, and measure the separation by fitting the
received left channel to the transmitted $L$ and $R$ by least squares
(@sec-signals-as-vectors): the ratio of the two coefficients is the crosstalk.

```{python}
LOWPASS_15K = signal.firwin(255, 15e3, fs=fs_mpx, window=("kaiser", 7.0))

def stereo_decode(m, theta, phase_error=0.0):
    """Mono sum M and difference D (both scaled back by the 0.9 of the composite) from the composite m and the pilot phase."""
    subcarrier = np.sin(2 * theta + phase_error)
    M = np.convolve(m, LOWPASS_15K, mode="same") / 0.9
    D = np.convolve(2 * m * subcarrier, LOWPASS_15K, mode="same") / 0.9
    return M, D

def separation_db(left, ref_L, ref_R, skip=7200):
    """Least-squares fit of the received channel on [L, R]; returns (crosstalk as a ratio in dB, SNR in dB)."""
    lag = align_lag(left, ref_L)
    e, rl, rr = (left[lag:], ref_L, ref_R) if lag >= 0 else (left, ref_L[-lag:], ref_R[-lag:])
    n = min(len(e), len(rl))
    A = np.column_stack([rl[skip:n], rr[skip:n]])
    coef, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(A, e[skip:n], rcond=None)
    residual = e[skip:n] - A @ coef
    return 20 * np.log10(abs(coef[0] / coef[1])), 10 * np.log10(np.sum((A @ coef) ** 2) / np.sum(residual ** 2))

def to_audio_rate(x):
    """From 240 kHz to 48 kHz: keep every fifth sample (the 15 kHz low-pass of the decoder has already filtered)."""
    return x[::5]

L_ref, R_ref = PROGRAMS["A"]
print(f"{'phase error':>12} {'separation':>11} {'tan^2(e/2)':>11}")
for deg in (0, 15, 30, 60):
    eps = np.radians(deg)
    M, D = stereo_decode(m_hat, theta_A, phase_error=eps)
    left = de_emphasis(to_audio_rate(M + D), fs_audio)
    sep, _ = separation_db(left, L_ref, R_ref)
    theory = -20 * np.log10(np.tan(eps / 2) ** 2) if deg else np.inf
    print(f"{deg:9d} deg {sep:8.1f} dB {theory:8.1f} dB")
    if deg:
        assert abs(sep - theory) < 1.0                              # @prp-stereo-phase
    else:
        assert sep > 40                                             # the loop's own phase error is tiny
```

The measured separation follows $\tan^2(\varepsilon/2)$ to within a decibel, and with the
loop's phase the stereo image of station A is excellent. The loop also settles
very fast, in a few milliseconds, but its transient distorts the start of the
audio, so we discard the first 0.15 s of every channel when we measure.

## Stage 7: the audio {#sec-sdr-audio}

What remains is simple. The decoder already filtered at 15 kHz, so reducing the rate
from 240 kHz to 48 kHz is keeping every fifth sample (@sec-multirate): a
second, much cheaper decimation stage. And the **de-emphasis** that cancels the
pre-emphasis of the station, which in the receiver also lowers the noise of the highest frequencies
(@sec-sdr-noise): it is the exact inverse of the filter of the transmitter,
so, together, they cancel. We assemble the whole chain in a function of the raw
bytes, which is the receiver.

```{python}
def receive_station(x, carrier, h=h_ch):
    """One station from the capture x (complex, 960 kS/s): stereo audio at 48 kHz and measurements."""
    m, residual = demodulate(select_channel(x, carrier, h))
    stereo_level = pilot_level_db(m)
    is_stereo = stereo_level > 15
    if is_stereo:
        theta, _, _ = pilot_pll(extract_pilot(m))
        M, D = stereo_decode(m, theta)
        L, R = M + D, M - D
    else:
        M = np.convolve(m, LOWPASS_15K, mode="same") / 0.9
        L = R = M
    audio = np.column_stack([de_emphasis(to_audio_rate(L), fs_audio), de_emphasis(to_audio_rate(R), fs_audio)])
    return {"audio": audio, "stereo": bool(is_stereo), "pilot_db": stereo_level, "offset": carrier, "residual_hz": residual}

def to_receiver_rate(x, rate):
    """Remove the DC offset of the tuner and, if the capture was made at another rate, resample it to fs_rf."""
    x = x - np.mean(x)
    if rate != fs_rf:
        ratio = Fraction(fs_rf, int(rate)).limit_denominator(1000)
        x = signal.resample_poly(x, ratio.numerator, ratio.denominator)
    return x

def fm_receiver(raw_bytes, rate=fs_rf, centres=CHANNELS):
    """The receiver: unsigned 8-bit I/Q bytes in (recorded at `rate` S/s, with stations on the grid `centres`),
    a list of stations with their stereo audio out."""
    x = to_receiver_rate(bytes_to_iq(raw_bytes), rate)
    f, P = psd_db(x, fs_rf)
    return [dict(receive_station(x, carrier), cnr_db=cnr) for carrier, cnr in scan_channels(f, P, centres=centres)]

stations_rx = fm_receiver(raw)
print(f"{'station':>8} {'carrier':>11} {'CNR':>8} {'type':>7} {'audio SNR L':>12} {'audio SNR R':>12}")
scores = {}
for name, st in zip("ABCD", stations_rx):
    L_ref, R_ref = PROGRAMS[name]
    snr_L = fit_snr_db(st["audio"][:, 0], L_ref, skip=7200)[0]
    snr_R = fit_snr_db(st["audio"][:, 1], R_ref, skip=7200)[0]
    scores[name] = (snr_L, snr_R)
    print(f"{name:>8} {st['offset'] / 1e3:8.1f} kHz {st['cnr_db']:5.1f} dB {'stereo' if st['stereo'] else 'mono':>7} {snr_L:9.1f} dB {snr_R:9.1f} dB")
assert [st["stereo"] for st in stations_rx] == [True, False, True, False]
assert min(scores["A"]) > 20 and min(scores["C"]) > 20 and min(scores["B"]) > 20
assert min(scores["D"]) > 8                                        # the faint station is noisy, but there
```

The receiver recognises that A and C are stereo and B and D mono, and recovers
the audio of each with a signal-to-noise ratio above 20 dB; station D, which is much closer to the
noise, comes out noisier. For the strong stations the limit is not
the radio noise: it is the distortion of squeezing the signal into a 200 kHz channel, which
we measure in @sec-sdr-noise. @fig-audio-rx compares what station A sent with what we received.

```{python}
#| label: fig-audio-rx
#| fig-cap: "Station A: the left (top) and right (bottom) channels that the station sent (blue) and what the receiver recovers (orange, scaled by the best gain and shifted by the delay of the chain), over 0.35 s. The two channels are different, and the receiver keeps them apart."
st_A = stations_rx[0]
L_ref, R_ref = PROGRAMS["A"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(7, 3.6), sharex=True)
for ax, ch, ref, label in ((axes[0], 0, L_ref, "left"), (axes[1], 1, R_ref, "right")):
    rx = st_A["audio"][:, ch]
    snr, lag, gain = fit_snr_db(rx, ref, skip=7200)
    n = min(len(rx) - max(lag, 0), len(ref) - max(-lag, 0))
    seg = slice(8000, 8000 + 16800)
    sent = ref[max(-lag, 0):][:n]
    got = rx[max(lag, 0):][:n] / gain
    tt = np.arange(n) / fs_audio
    ax.plot(tt[seg], sent[seg], lw=0.8, label="sent")
    ax.plot(tt[seg], got[seg], lw=0.8, label="received")
    ax.set(ylabel=label)
axes[0].legend(fontsize=7, loc="upper right")
axes[1].set_xlabel("time [s]")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
```{python}
Clips({f"What station {name} sent": np.column_stack(PROGRAMS[name]) for name in "AD"}
      | {f"What the receiver heard of station {name}": st["audio"] / np.max(np.abs(st["audio"]))
         for name, st in zip("ABCD", stations_rx) if name in "AD"}, fs_audio)
```

Listen to the received station D: it is the faint one, and you can hear the noise
that a weak signal brings, a hiss that rises with frequency, as we are going to
see in the next section.
